baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Interprets Reconstruction through Black political action, contested freedom and the struggle to build democracy.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own interview answers stress change after slavery and oppose treating later injustice as proof that emancipation changed nothing.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Traces competing meanings of freedom rather than treating freedom as one stable national possession.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: In the interview Foner explicitly contrasts economic equality and rights with narrow anti-government definitions, and rejects narratives that absorb every struggle into a stable Americanism.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Foner explicitly identifies Black Reconstruction and Du Bois’s account of the Civil War as resources for his interpretation of emancipation and revolution.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Foner’s own 2015 answers recount using Black Reconstruction and expressly identify his agreement with Du Bois. This is a bounded acknowledgment, not proof of every influence on Foner or a claim that his family acquaintance alone establishes intellectual transmission.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Questions the comparative scope of Foner’s Reconstruction while praising its achievement and correcting any implication that Foner lacked comparative expertise.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Woodward’s May1988 review urges comparisons with other emancipations; his June correction explicitly credits Foner’s Nothing But Freedom(1983). The criticism concerns the larger book’s scope, not ignorance of comparison. Foner’s books remain unread here; praise, qualification and the correction belong to one bounded critical reception.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Criticizes Woodward’s earlier tendency to portray African Americans as victims rather than historical agents, while valuing his engaged scholarship.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Foner’s own2022 review contrasts Woodward’s previous writing with later grassroots Reconstruction scholarship and ends by crediting his public achievement. This is a particular historiographical criticism, not dismissal of the whole corpus. Woodward’s original books and Cobb’s complete biography remain unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Foner praises Davis’s trilogy but questions speculative psychological dehumanization and notes that the book’s fugitive-slave evidence challenges its generalization.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2014review distinguishes racial dehumanization as a legal/social practice from claims of internalized psychological damage. Foner values Davis’s treatment of free Black leadership and contingency while making this objection. The criticism targets the2014volume’s argument; no dismissal of the trilogy or whole-book reading claimed.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Defends the regional and chronological scope of Slaves Without Masters against Ely’s reported charge that Berlin equates restrictive law with daily life.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2004 Foner review permits generalizations, regional comparisons and change over1790–1860 that a single-county study cannot provide, while valuing Ely’s local research. This is an explicitly bounded reception intervention; it neither certifies all Berlin findings nor credits Berlin with writing Foner’s reply. Original books unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Lears uses Foner’s account of artisans and price controls to show contradictions within producer ideology.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own575locates the shift from communal moral economy toward entrepreneurial expectations in Foner’s research. Plural surrounding reconstruction includes Laurie, Dawley, Hahn and Wilentz. Cited Tom Paine and Revolutionary America1976pp41,157 and chapter5; complete original unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: McPherson uses Foner’s account of fugitive slaves and interracial aid networks to explain how a numerically small movement intensified sectional conflict.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own 2015 review endorses the political force of escapees and publicizes Foner’s New York evidence. Madeline Lewis’s discovery of Gay’s Record of Fugitives, Gay and Louis Napoleon’s work and enslaved people’s initiative retain credit. Specific resource in this essay, not a claim that Foner originated McPherson’s broader emancipation interpretation. Full Gateway to Freedom and record independently unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Credits Foner as her adviser and a central model for historical scholarship, teaching and public engagement.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Her own acknowledgment on p. xv calls Foner her adviser and her biggest debt, while also naming other Columbia teachers. Her 1999 article, p. 67, acknowledges support and constructive criticism. No single proprietary theory, sole authorship or independently inspected degree file is inferred. The acknowledgment was read in the 2014 reprint; the 2004 printing was not collated.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Critically reworks the economic-conflict interpretation and explores ideological consensus in American politics.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Foner distinguishes Hofstadter’s critical consensus interpretation from celebratory versions and notes the later reconsideration of conflict.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Brings status anxiety, symbols and irrationality into accounts of political culture.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Foner’s named substantive reading also judges the treatment of Populists and Progressives exaggerated and elitist in important respects. This qualification survives the contribution arrow.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: As Foner recounts, defends the Populists’ corporate critique against Hofstadter’s emphasis on conspiracy and cultural hatreds.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Explicit named scholarly mediation: Foner’s2022 review, paragraphs beginning For decades and It was a book, distinguishes their disagreement from friendship. It also notes Woodward later conceded exaggerating white Populists’ racial egalitarianism. Original exchanges and complete books remain unread; editorial collaboration does not erase this disagreement.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Davis adapts Freudian transference, through Erikson’s Gandhi’s Truth, as one explanation for metropolitan British concern with distant slavery.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated by Manisha Sinha (2019), p. 151/n. 25: she identifies Davis’s admiration for Erik H. Erikson’s 1969 book and his application of transference in Age of Revolution. Erikson retains the intermediary credit; no direct Freud reading or whole-book method is asserted. Sinha criticizes this psychological explanation; Foner separately criticizes a later Freudian excursion, without documenting the same transmission chain. Freud, Erikson and Davis originals remain unread.
